subject: history
subtitle: Understanding how historians organise and measure time across historical periods.

data.targetWord: the arrangement of events in the order in which they occurred over time

examples.en-GB: Good chronology helps historians avoid muddled explanations of cause and consequence.

data.targetWord: a visual or written line that places events in date order to show sequence and change

examples.en-GB: The classroom timeline showed events from 1066 to the present day.

data.targetWord: the order of events from the earliest to the latest

examples.en-GB: The correct sequence places the Norman Conquest before Magna Carta.

data.targetWord: a block of time given a label by historians to help organise the past, such as the medieval period

examples.en-GB: The medieval period is roughly dated from c.1066 to c.1500 in British history.

data.targetWord: a long period of history characterised by a shared feature or dominant theme, such as the Victorian era

examples.en-GB: The Victorian era lasted from 1837 to 1901 and is associated with empire and industrialisation.

data.targetWord: a period of one hundred years; the name of a century is one number ahead of the first two digits of most years within it

examples.en-GB: The year 1832 falls in the 19th century, which covers the years 1801 to 1900.

data.targetWord: a period of ten years, often used to describe a distinct cultural or political phase

examples.en-GB: The 1960s are often associated with cultural change and youth movements in Britain.

data.targetWord: a period of one thousand years

examples.en-GB: Farming developed over many millennia in different parts of the world.

data.targetWord: the length of time that something lasted from its beginning to its end

examples.en-GB: The duration of Elizabeth I's reign was about 45 years, from 1558 to 1603.

data.targetWord: the gap in time between two events or dates

examples.en-GB: The interval between the Black Death in 1348 and the Peasants' Revolt in 1381 is 33 years.

data.targetWord: an event or development that leads to significant and lasting change in society, government, or everyday life

examples.en-GB: The Norman Conquest of 1066 is often described as a turning point because it changed England's ruling class and land ownership.

data.targetWord: from or belonging to the same period of time; when used of people, it means they lived at the same time

examples.en-GB: Henry VIII and Martin Luther were broadly contemporary because they lived during the same period.

data.targetWord: something placed in the wrong time period, such as an object, idea or word that did not yet exist at the time shown

examples.en-GB: Showing a medieval knight using a mobile phone would be a clear anachronism.

data.targetWord: dating system for years after the traditional starting point; AD means Anno Domini and CE means Common Era — both count the same years

examples.en-GB: The Roman conquest of Britain began in AD 43, which is the same as 43 CE.

data.targetWord: dating system for years before the traditional starting point; BC means Before Christ and BCE means Before Common Era — in this system, larger numbers are earlier

examples.en-GB: Julius Caesar's first expedition to Britain was in 55 BC, which is earlier than AD 43.

data.targetWord: the historical period in Britain roughly from c.1066 to c.1500, associated with castles, feudalism, Church authority, and limited royal government by modern standards

examples.en-GB: Medieval England was characterised by feudal land holding and the great power of the Catholic Church.

data.targetWord: the historical period in Britain roughly from c.1500 to c.1750, associated with Tudor and Stuart monarchy, the Reformation, exploration and the growth of Parliament

examples.en-GB: The English Civil War of 1642 falls in the early modern period.

data.targetWord: the period of major economic and social change roughly from c.1750 to c.1900, when Britain shifted from agriculture to factory production, and towns and railways grew rapidly

examples.en-GB: During the Industrial Revolution, cities like Manchester grew rapidly as workers moved to find factory jobs.

data.targetWord: the process of dividing the past into named periods or eras to help organise historical study, even though these divisions are simplified

examples.en-GB: Periodisation is useful, but historians remind us that changes overlap and do not happen on one exact date.

data.targetWord: aspects of life, society or government that remained the same or changed very little over a period of time

examples.en-GB: Despite the Norman Conquest, continuity can be seen in the farming routines of ordinary villagers.

data.targetWord: differences in society, government, technology, beliefs or daily life between one period and another

examples.en-GB: The introduction of the NHS in 1948 represented a significant change in access to healthcare in Britain.

data.targetWord: the military invasion of England in 1066 led by William of Normandy, which changed England's ruling class, land ownership, government, and links with continental Europe

examples.en-GB: The Norman Conquest of 1066 is often described as the most significant turning point in medieval English history.

data.targetWord: a document agreed by King John and rebellious barons in 1215 that placed some limits on royal power and later became symbolically important in the history of law and rights

examples.en-GB: Although Magna Carta in 1215 mainly protected elite interests, later generations used it as a symbol of limits on monarchy.

data.targetWord: a devastating outbreak of plague that reached England in 1348-1349, killing a large part of the population and contributing to changes in labour, wages and social relations

examples.en-GB: The Black Death of 1348-1349 reduced the population so sharply that labour became scarcer and some workers could demand higher wages.

data.targetWord: the 1534 law by which Henry VIII declared himself head of the Church of England, breaking with the authority of the Pope in Rome

examples.en-GB: The Act of Supremacy of 1534 marked a turning point because it changed both religion and royal power in England.

data.targetWord: a law passed in 1689 after the Glorious Revolution that limited royal power and strengthened the authority of Parliament

examples.en-GB: The Bill of Rights of 1689 helped shift power from the monarch towards Parliament.

data.targetWord: the 1832 law that changed parliamentary representation and widened the vote to a larger group of men in Britain

examples.en-GB: The Great Reform Act of 1832 was an important step in the gradual extension of voting rights in Britain.

data.targetWord: the publicly funded healthcare system established in Britain in 1948, making medical treatment available according to need rather than ability to pay

examples.en-GB: The creation of the National Health Service in 1948 represented a major turning point in welfare and public health.

data.targetWord: Duke of Normandy who defeated Harold Godwinson at the Battle of Hastings in 1066 and became King William I of England, ordering the Domesday Book

examples.en-GB: William the Conqueror ordered the Domesday Book in 1086 to record land, people and wealth across England.

data.targetWord: a detailed survey of land, people and wealth in England, commissioned by William I and completed in 1086, used for royal government and taxation

examples.en-GB: The Domesday Book of 1086 is a primary source that tells historians about land ownership and wealth in Norman England.

data.targetWord: Tudor queen of England from 1558 to 1603, whose reign is associated with religious settlement, conflict with Spain, exploration, and theatre

examples.en-GB: Elizabeth I's reign lasted 45 years and is often seen as a high point of Tudor power.

data.targetWord: the period during which a monarch rules a country

examples.en-GB: Queen Victoria's reign lasted from 1837 to 1901, a duration of about 64 years.

data.title: Is each statement about period labels an advantage or a limitation?

pairs.text: They help organise large amounts of time and make the past easier to study
They allow historians to group events and compare different societies
They can make change look sudden, as if one period ended on a single day
They can hide different experiences of women, poorer people and colonised peoples
They provide a shared vocabulary that students and historians can use together
Different places changed at different speeds, so one label may not fit all areas equally
